justification: The article is a clean shape-B build-up across exactly the arc CONTENT_PLAN.md row 7 specifies and the task described: an unheaded intro (hard-coded SmtpReceiptSender field) -> 'Passing the dependency in by hand' (constructor injection) -> 'Wiring the whole graph: the composition root' (four-type diamond graph + Figure 1) -> 'Lifetimes: transient, scoped, and singleton, precisely' (+ Figure 2) -> 'A container that resolves the graph, in about sixty lines' (MiniContainer) -> 'The same graph, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection' (same four booleans, real package) -> 'The captive dependency: a singleton that outlives its scope' (bug, validation, fix). Every section's code, the two diagrams, and the two exercises revolve around the same InvoiceService/IReceiptSender/IAuditLog/IClock graph throughout -- no drive-by unrelated examples. Headings are specific, no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion, no restated-heading summary. The two required diagrams are both present and strong: Figure 1 (object graph, viewBox 300x500, portrait, well under the 360 cap) shows the four-type dependency graph with a dashed accent path from InvoiceService directly to SystemClock closing the diamond exactly as the brief specifies, correct aria-labelledby/title/desc, class-only coloring, renders legibly and with correct contrast in both light and dark mobile screenshots I opened; Figure 2 (lifetime scopes, viewBox 320x520) correctly shows one Singleton band shared by two Scope boxes each holding a scoped instance plus two transients, with a dashed accent line showing the singleton reaching the second scope without being rebuilt -- exactly the lifetime semantics the adjacent prose defines. Both figures have captions that state what to notice and were confirmed, by direct read of the raw Markdown, to contain zero blank lines between (the known past bug). The two exercises are well-formed and correctly varied per WRITER_GUIDE.md: 'Find the missed injection' is a prose-only find-the-bug (no output shown, solution collapsed in :::solution) and 'Predict a forgotten reuse' is a genuine predict-the-output -- the question describes the code change in prose without showing the modified program or its output, and both the modified program and its `text output` block are correctly placed inside the :::solution, so nothing leaks under the question. That is real form variety within one article, an explicit improvement over the sibling factory-builder-singleton review's finding that all three of its exercises were the same 'explain in prose' shape. The :::warning and :::dotnet callouts are both used per WRITER_GUIDE.md convention (a titled warning flagging that the captive-dependency program ran without error, and a :::dotnet callout citing the IServiceScopeFactory-is-always-a-singleton fact) and render correctly in the screenshots with their respective icon/label/accent-bar styling, visually distinct from each other and from the exercise boxes. All 18 code fences use `csharp run [id=]` correctly per tools/run-code.mjs -- no sql/bash blocks, no xUnit in this article, `#:package Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection@9.*` used correctly for the two MSDI blocks, every `text output` block sits directly after its `run` block with no interposed content, and the real verify-page run's own code=18/fig=2 counts confirm nothing is malformed enough to be silently dropped. Lighthouse is a real, freshly-run 100/100/100/100, zero console errors, zero broken links (internal or external), zero mobile horizontal overflow. The one concrete defect, worth a fraction of a point but not a pass-blocker, is exactly the block the brief flagged as a risk: inside `csharp run id=mini-container-demo` (the ~60-line MiniContainer block), the four `container.Register<...>(Lifetime.X)` calls on md lines 376-379 are 60-74 columns wide with the varying `Lifetime.Singleton`/`.Scoped`/`.Transient` argument -- the entire point of that four-line block, since it is what proves all three lifetimes are wired -- starting at column 43, 50, 58 and 54 respectively, all past the ~40-column visible boundary on a 390px phone. I confirmed this directly in the mobile-light-part08.png screenshot: all four lines are visibly truncated mid-token before the lifetime value is readable, whereas the equivalent MSDI block a few sections later (`services.AddSingleton();` etc.) does not have this problem, because that API bakes the lifetime into the method name near the start of the line instead of a trailing enum argument. A phone reader working through the block that is explicitly introduced as demonstrating 'all three lifetimes' cannot see which lifetime each registration uses without scrolling sideways.

issues.location: `csharp run id=mini-container-demo` block, md lines 376-379: the four `container.Register<...>(Lifetime.X);` calls
issues.problem: Each line is 60-74 columns, and the argument that varies and matters -- `Lifetime.Singleton` / `Lifetime.Scoped` / `Lifetime.Transient` (x2) -- starts at column 43-58, past the ~40-column visible boundary on a 390px phone screenshot. Confirmed in mobile-light-part08.png: all four lines are visibly cut off before the lifetime value is legible. This is the demo block's entire point (registering the same four-type graph with all three lifetimes at once), so the fact a phone reader has to scroll sideways to see which lifetime each line uses undercuts the block's purpose more than an arbitrary long line would.
issues.fixLooksLike: Break each call across two lines so the lifetime argument starts near column 8-12, e.g. `container.Register<IClock, SystemClock>(\n    Lifetime.Singleton);`, or shorten the type-argument pairs (a `using` alias is not idiomatic here, but wrapping after the closing `>` reliably gets the lifetime onto the visible part of its own line for all four registrations).
